The Barred parakeet Bolborhynchus lineola is a small Neotropical parrot inhabiting montane forests from southern Mexico to Peru. Studies of captive breeding colonies have provided detailed data on its early development and reproductive biology. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after a remarkably precise incubation period of approximately 21.5 days [ab = approximately 21.5 days], a duration typical for psittacines of this modest body size. The wet weight at birth of the newly emerged hatchling is a mere 2.32 grams [Wwb = 2.32 grams], reflecting the altricial state of the neonate, which emerges with closed eyes and sparse down. This minimal mass at hatching stands in contrast to the species' ultimate adult size, as the wet weight at birth constitutes only a small fraction of the maximum adult body mass. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg has been measured at approximately 3.93 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.93 grams], indicating that the developing embryo undergoes a net loss of mass during incubation as it metabolizes yolk and albumen reserves.

The nestling phase of the Barred parakeet is characterized by rapid mass gain and feather development under the consistent thermal conditions maintained by the brooding adult. When reared at the typical nest-cavity temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones is observed. The age at fledging, when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest cavity, occurs at 32 days since birth [tx = 32 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This fledging period is relatively compressed compared to larger-bodied parrots, a pattern linked to the need to minimize nest predation risk in open montane habitats. The chick's growth trajectory during this interval is steep, transforming a 2.32-gram hatchling into a fully feathered juvenile capable of independent locomotion. Nestlings are provisioned intensively by both parents, with crop milk and pre-digested seeds forming the primary diet during the first two weeks of the brooding period.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds at a moderate pace relative to other small parrots, with gonadal development occurring under the same thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods. Puberty is attained at 96 days since birth [tp = 96 days since birth] when maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], marking the onset of reproductive competence in both males and females. This relatively early pubertal age, roughly three months after fledging, is consistent with the rapid life-history strategy observed in many small-bodied Neotropical psittacines. However, despite reaching physiological maturity at this age, the first successful brood is not usually attempted until the following breeding season. The transition from physiological puberty to actual breeding is mediated by social and environmental cues, including photoperiod and food availability.

The timing of first successful reproduction in the Barred parakeet appears to be closely linked to the species' montane environment and its pronounced seasonal cycles. The age at first brood is 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] under the standard temperature conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], effectively aligning the initiation of breeding with the second breeding season following the bird's own hatching. This delay between the attainment of puberty at 96 days and the first successful brood at 365 days likely reflects the time required for territory acquisition, mate selection, and the development of foraging proficiency sufficient to support the energetic demands of egg production and chick provisioning. The adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, attained by fully grown Barred parakeets is approximately 55.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 55.7 grams], a measurement that places the species among the smaller members of the Arini tribe.

Reproductive output in the Barred parakeet is characterized by a relatively modest clutch size and a single annual breeding attempt in most wild populations, though captive conditions can alter this pattern. Females typically produce a clutch of 2 eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting event], and field records indicate that they raise approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year] during the extended breeding season of the montane cloud forest, resulting in a maximum daily reproduction rate of 4 eggs per year [Ri = 4 eggs per year] though this frequency may be reduced at higher elevations. The maximum recorded longevity for the species, documented from banded individuals in both wild and captive settings, is approximately 15.2 years [am = approximately 15.2 years] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This lifespan, measured under the thermal conditions of the species' native habitat at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], is considerable for a bird of such small body mass and suggests a slow pace of aging relative to similarly sized passerines, perhaps linked to the relatively protected nesting environment of cavity-dwelling parrots.
